guide.title: Application guide
guide.intro: An application is one of the platform's apps or portals, such as the Rider app or the Ops portal. Organizations are given access to applications, and security policies, API clients and roles can be set per application.

fields.title: What each field means
fields.code: Pick it from the platform catalogue. It cannot be changed later; applications already created are greyed out.
fields.name: The name and description users see. When several organizations share the application, only a super admin can change them.
fields.baseUrl: The address where the application runs, e.g. https://ops.example.com.
fields.landingPage: The page users open after signing in, e.g. /dashboard.
fields.supportEmail: The help contact for this application.
fields.type: Set by the catalogue entry, e.g. WEB or MOBILE, and cannot be changed here.

auth.title: Authentication mode
auth.text: How users of this application prove who they are. Change it only together with the platform team: a wrong mode stops everyone from signing in.
auth.LOCAL: Accounts and passwords kept by the platform. The usual choice.
auth.KEYCLOAK: Sign-in through the platform's Keycloak server.
auth.OAUTH2: Sign-in through an outside provider using OAuth 2.0.
auth.OIDC: Sign-in through an outside provider using OpenID Connect.
auth.LDAP: The company directory (LDAP or Active Directory).
auth.CUSTOM: A custom integration agreed with the platform team.

example.title: Example
example.text: To bring the Driver app onto the platform: pick its code from the catalogue, keep the name, set the base URL, landing page and support email, and leave the mode on LOCAL. Then give the organizations that use it access, and add an application-level security policy if drivers need different rules.

errors.clientId: Use 3 to 64 letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens, starting with a letter or digit. No spaces or other symbols.

guide.title: How this screen works
guide.intro: An API client lets another system or app call this platform's APIs. Save it here, then the system uses the client ID and secret to get an access token.

steps.title: Steps
steps.text: 1. Enter a Client ID and choose the organization. 2. Pick a Client Type; the matching authentication method and grant types are filled in. 3. Add scopes (and redirect URIs only if AUTHORIZATION_CODE is ticked). 4. Save and copy the secret straight away. It is shown only once. Use Rotate Secret in the list if you need a new one.

clientType.title: Client Type
clientType.text: What kind of system uses this client.
clientType.integration: A partner or outside system calling our APIs. Signs in as itself (CLIENT_CREDENTIALS).
clientType.internal: One of our own back-end services or scheduled jobs. Signs in as itself (CLIENT_CREDENTIALS).
clientType.browser: A web or mobile app where a person signs in. Uses AUTHORIZATION_CODE and REFRESH_TOKEN, and needs redirect URIs.

authMethod.title: Authentication Method
authMethod.clientSecret: The client sends its ID and secret when asking for a token. The secret is generated when you save.
authMethod.notYet: Listed for the future but not set up yet, so they can't be picked.

grantTypes.title: Grant Types
grantTypes.clientCredentials: System-to-system. No user involved. Use this for external integrations.
grantTypes.authorizationCode: A person signs in through the browser and is sent back to a redirect URI.
grantTypes.refreshToken: Lets a signed-in app get a new token without asking the person to sign in again.
grantTypes.password: The app sends the person's username and password directly. Avoid unless there is no other option.
grantTypes.deviceCode: Sign-in on devices without a keyboard (TVs, kiosks). Not set up in Keycloak yet.

other.title: Other fields
other.tenant: The organization the client belongs to. Its tokens are issued by that organization's realm. Leave empty for the default realm.
other.application: Optional: the application this client is for.
other.scopes: What the tokens may access. Give an outside system only what it needs.
other.redirectUris: Where the browser returns after sign-in. Only used with AUTHORIZATION_CODE; must be https except for localhost.

token.title: Getting a token
token.text: POST to {keycloak}/realms/railcab-<organization code>/protocol/openid-connect/token with grant_type=client_credentials, client_id, client_secret and scope. Send the returned access_token as "Authorization: Bearer <token>" on each API call.

securityPolicies.activationHint: Saving an active policy applies it immediately. Affected sessions must sign in again. Users without an authenticator will set one up during sign-in when MFA is mandatory.
securityPolicies.savedValuesHint: These are the currently saved rules for the selected scope. Unsaved edits are not included.

guide.title: Security policy guide
guide.intro: A security policy sets the password, sign-in, session, two-step sign-in and account rules for the whole platform, one organization or one application. Any setting can be left on Inherit.

combine.title: How policies combine
combine.text: Each user gets the platform rules, then their organization's, then their application's. For every setting the stricter value wins, so a lower level can tighten a rule but never relax it. Preview saved policy shows the result and where each value comes from.
combine.global: Organization and application both left blank. Applies to everyone.
combine.org: Only an organization chosen. Applies to all of its applications.
combine.app: Organization and application chosen. Applies only to sign-ins to that application.
combine.inherit: The setting is taken from the level above, or the platform default.

scope.title: Who it applies to
scope.name: A clear name your team will recognise, e.g. "Franchise staff – Rider app".
scope.description: Why the policy exists and what it changes, so the next admin understands it.
scope.tenant: The organization the policy covers. Leave blank for a platform-wide policy.
scope.application: The application it covers, e.g. BestRide Rider. Leave blank to cover every application of the organization.

password.title: Password rules
password.minLength: Shortest password allowed, 8 to 128 characters. 12 or more is recommended for staff.
password.maxLength: Longest password allowed; it cannot be less than the minimum. The platform default is 72.
password.upper: Yes: at least one capital letter (A–Z), e.g. "Ride2026!".
password.lower: Yes: at least one small letter (a–z).
password.number: Yes: at least one digit (0–9). The platform requires this by default.
password.special: Yes: at least one symbol, such as ! @ # $ %.
password.username: Yes: the password may not contain the user's username, e.g. user "ravi" cannot use "ravi@123".
password.history: How many of the user's last passwords cannot be reused, e.g. 5. 0 turns this off.
password.minAge: Days before a new password can be changed again, so users cannot cycle back to an old one, e.g. 1. 0 turns this off.
password.expiry: Days after which the password must be changed, e.g. 90. 0 means it never expires.

login.title: Sign-in protection
login.maxFailed: Wrong passwords allowed in a row before the account locks, 1 to 20, e.g. 5 (the platform default).
login.lockDuration: How long a locked account stays locked, in minutes, e.g. 30. The platform default is 15.
login.allowConcurrent: Yes: the same user may be signed in on several devices at once. No: one device at a time.
login.maxConcurrent: When several are allowed, the most devices at once, e.g. 3 (phone, laptop, tablet). 0 means no limit.

session.title: Sessions
session.idle: Minutes without activity before the user is signed out, at least 1, e.g. 30.
session.absolute: The longest a session can last in minutes, active or not, e.g. 720 for a 12-hour shift. Then the user signs in again.
session.single: Yes: signing in on a new device ends the user's other sessions.
session.onPassword: Yes: after a password change, every open session must sign in again. On by default.
session.onRole: Yes: after a role change, the user signs in again so the new access applies. On by default.

mfa.title: Two-step sign-in (MFA)
mfa.enabled: Yes: users may add a second step (a one-time code) to their sign-in.
mfa.mandatory: Yes: every user must use a second step; anyone without one sets it up while signing in. Needs Authenticator App Allowed.
mfa.email: Yes: the code may be sent to the user's email.
mfa.sms: Yes: the code may be sent by SMS to the user's mobile.
mfa.app: Yes: the code may come from an authenticator app such as Google or Microsoft Authenticator. Required when MFA is mandatory.

account.title: Accounts
account.selfRegistration: Yes: people may create their own account, e.g. riders signing up in the app. No: only admins create accounts.
account.email: Yes: a new account must confirm its email address before it can be used.
account.phone: Yes: a new account must confirm its mobile number with an OTP.
account.approval: Yes: a new account stays pending until an admin approves it.

activation.title: When it applies
activation.active: On: the policy is in force. Saving an active policy applies at once and affected users sign in again. Off: kept but ignored.
activation.from: Optional start in UTC, e.g. 2026-12-01T09:00:00. Empty: from now.
activation.until: Optional end in UTC, e.g. 2027-03-31T23:59:59. Empty: no end.

example.title: Example
example.text: Franchise staff use the BestRide Rider app. Choose Default organization and BestRide Rider, then set minimum length 12, require uppercase, lowercase, number and symbol, 5 failed attempts with a 30-minute lock, a 30-minute idle timeout, and MFA mandatory with the authenticator app allowed. Users of the organization's other applications keep the organization's rules.

deleteDialog.title: Delete Notification Template?

guide.title: Notification template guide
guide.intro: A template is the wording of one message the platform sends (an OTP, a welcome email, an assignment alert) for one channel and one language. Services send a code and values; the template turns them into the message.

fields.title: What each field means
fields.code: The code services send, e.g. USER_WELCOME. It must match the sending service exactly. Add one template per channel and language you need.
fields.name: A readable name and description for admins, e.g. "Welcome email".
fields.tenant: An organization id for wording specific to one organization. Leave empty for the platform-wide default.
fields.application: An application id for wording specific to one app. Leave empty to use it for all apps.
fields.language: The language of this text. Add a template for each language your users use.
fields.subject: The email subject or push title, e.g. "Welcome to {{organizationName}}".
fields.body: The message itself. Put each value in double curly braces, e.g. "Hi {{name}}, your code is {{otp}}." The organization's name is always available as {{organizationName}}.
fields.variables: The names of the values the text uses, e.g. name, otp. The sending service must send every one, or the message shows a gap.

channels.title: Channels
channels.EMAIL: An email; can be long and formatted (choose HTML).
channels.SMS: A text message; keep it short, as long messages are split and cost more.
channels.PUSH: A notification on the phone; a short title and one or two lines.
channels.WHATSAPP: A WhatsApp message; providers usually need the wording approved first.
channels.IN_APP: A message inside the app's notification list.

engines.title: Template engine
engines.text: Values such as {{name}} are filled in for every engine. The engine mainly says how the text is formatted.
engines.PLAIN_TEXT: Plain text, for SMS, push and simple emails.
engines.HTML: Formatted email with headings, links and images.
engines.THYMELEAF: An HTML template in Thymeleaf form, for teams that already use it.
engines.FREEMARKER: An HTML template in FreeMarker form, for teams that already use it.
engines.MUSTACHE: A Mustache template; the same {{name}} style.

example.text: A welcome SMS in Telugu: code USER_WELCOME, channel SMS, language TE, engine PLAIN_TEXT, body in Telugu with {{name}} and {{organizationName}}, variables name. Add a second template with language EN for English speakers.

guide.title: User guide
guide.intro: A user is one sign-in account. Its roles decide what the person may do; its organization memberships decide whose data they see.

before.title: Before you start
before.text: Search the users list first: one person should have one account, even across several organizations. To give an existing person access to another organization, add them in that organization's Members section instead of creating a second account.

fields.title: What each field means
fields.username: The name used to sign in, unique on the whole platform, e.g. ravi.kumar.
fields.password: Needed for a new user: at least 8 characters with a letter and a number, e.g. Welcome2026. Leave it empty when editing to keep the current one. Share it privately and ask the person to change it after the first sign-in.
fields.fullName: How the person appears on screens and in history, e.g. Ravi Kumar.
fields.userType: The kind of account (codes below). It labels the person; what they may do comes only from their roles.
fields.email: Used for sign-in codes, password resets and notifications, e.g. ravi.kumar@company.com.
fields.phone: Needed for a new user; used for SMS codes. Pick the country first, then the number.
fields.roles: Give the smallest set of roles that lets the person do the job. A change applies the next time they sign in.

types.title: User types
types.SUPER_ADMIN: Full control of the whole platform and every organization. Keep this to a very few trusted people.
types.ADMIN: Runs an organization: its users, roles and settings.
types.OPS: Operations staff who work the daily queues.
types.CUSTOMER: A customer or rider of the apps.
types.VENDOR: A vendor or partner company's user.

statuses.title: Statuses
statuses.INACTIVE: Switched off for now; cannot sign in.
statuses.PENDING: Waiting for approval or for email or phone verification.
statuses.LOCKED: Locked after too many wrong passwords. It unlocks after the lock time, or when an admin sets it back to ACTIVE.
statuses.SUSPENDED: Blocked for a while, e.g. during an investigation.
statuses.DISABLED: Switched off for good, e.g. the person has left. The history is kept.

practice.title: Good practice
practice.text: Prefer SUSPENDED or DISABLED to deleting: the account's history stays in the audit trail. Review who holds SUPER_ADMIN and ADMIN regularly, and remove roles people no longer need.

example.title: Example
example.text: A new operations agent joins the franchise desk: username anita.rao, full name Anita Rao, type OPS, her work email and mobile, role "Operations agent", status ACTIVE. Send the temporary password privately and ask her to change it after her first sign-in.

guide.title: Role guide
guide.intro: A role is a named set of permissions, such as "Disputes manager". You give roles to users; a user can hold several, and can do everything those roles allow together.

details.title: Role details
details.code: Capital letters, digits and _, starting with a letter, 3 to 50 characters and unique on the platform, e.g. DISPUTES_MANAGER. Keep it unchanged once people hold the role.
details.name: What people see in lists, e.g. Disputes manager.
details.description: What the role is for, e.g. "Handles refund disputes for the Vijayawada region".
details.system: Only for platform-wide administrators. It makes the role shared by every organization, and an organization's own admins cannot change or delete it. Leave it off for a role of one organization.

levels.title: Access levels
levels.text: In the simple view, open an area and choose a level for each feature.
levels.none: The role cannot see the feature.
levels.view: Can look at lists and records, but cannot change anything.
levels.manage: Can look, create, change and delete.
levels.custom: Only some of the feature's actions are on; they were chosen in the advanced view.

quick.text: These apply to the category, application and service selected above; search only narrows the list.
quick.readOnly: Sets every feature to View: a safe start for auditors and supervisors.
quick.fullAccess: Sets every feature to Manage. Use it with care.
quick.clear: Turns everything off, to start again.

advanced.text: Lists every technical permission code with filters, to switch single actions on or off. Codes ending in _LIST or _READ only look; codes ending in _CREATE, _UPDATE, _DELETE or _MANAGE change data.

practice.title: Good practice
practice.text: Build roles around jobs, not people. Start from View and add Manage only where the job needs it. A change reaches each holder at their next sign-in. Permissions for a new feature belong to no role except SUPER_ADMIN until you add them here.

example.text: A role for the disputes team: code DISPUTES_MANAGER, name Disputes manager. In the simple view set the refunds feature to Manage, customer records to View and leave everything else on None. Save, then give the role to the team on the Users screen.

legal.entityType: Sole proprietor, partnership, company and so on; it decides which registrations apply.
legal.legalName: Exactly as written on the registration certificate.

kyc.identity: Needed. E.g. passport, Aadhaar, voter ID or driving licence.
kyc.address: Needed. E.g. a recent utility bill, Aadhaar or a rent agreement.
kyc.business: When the franchise is a registered business: its registration certificate.
kyc.tax: When it is registered for tax: the tax registration certificate.
kyc.submitted: Uploaded and waiting for an administrator to check it.

desk.summary: The service desk is the team's shared queue of requests and incidents. Each ticket gets a number (like OPS-42), a priority with a target time, a queue (team) and the person working on it.
desk.p1: Click New ticket and give it a short title, a category (Incident, Request, Problem, Change or Question), a queue and a priority. If you leave Due by empty, the priority sets it: Urgent 4 h, High 8 h, Normal 24 h, Low 72 h.
desk.p2: Use the queues (My work, Unassigned, Team queue, Raised by me, Resolved), the filters and search to find tickets. The counters at the top show your open, unassigned, overdue and urgent tickets.
desk.p3: Switch between List and Board. On the board, drag a card between Open, In progress, Waiting and Resolved to change its status.
desk.p4: Open a ticket to edit it, take it with Assign to me, or add a comment. Every change is kept in its history, and the person assigned is notified.
desk.p5: Write what fixed it when you Resolve a ticket, and Close it once the requester confirms.
desk.e1: A franchise reports "Payouts for 14 Nov not received". You create OPS-57: category Incident, queue Finance, priority High, so it is due in 8 hours.
desk.e2: Anita from Finance finds it under Unassigned, clicks Assign to me and then Start work.
desk.e3: She comments "Bank file was rejected, sent again at 15:10" and moves it to Waiting until the bank confirms.
desk.e4: Next morning she resolves it with "Payout credited after the file was re-sent" and closes it once the franchise confirms.

todos.summary: My to-dos is your own checklist for the day. Only you can see these items.
todos.p1: Type what you need to do and press Add. Choose a quick due time (Today 6 PM, Tomorrow 9 AM, Next Monday) or a date, and a priority.
todos.p2: The list is grouped into Overdue, Due today, This week, Later and No due date, with the most urgent first in each group.
todos.p3: Tick an item to mark it done. Select several and use Mark done to finish them together. Show done brings finished items back.
todos.p4: Search and the priority filter narrow a long list. Edit or delete an item from its row.
todos.e1: At 9:00 you add "Call Kumar Travels about the pending KYC" with Today 6 PM and priority High.
todos.e2: It sits at the top of Due today. After the call you tick it off and it moves to Done.
todos.e3: You also add "Prepare the weekly payout report" for Next Monday; it waits under This week or Later until then.

tasks.summary: Team tasks are pieces of work you give to a colleague, or take yourself, and follow up on together.
tasks.p1: Add a task with a title, a due date and a priority, and pick who does it from the people list. They are notified when it is assigned to them.
tasks.p2: Use All, Assigned to me, Created by me and Unassigned to see whose work it is.
tasks.p3: Click the speech bubble on a task to open its comments. The creator and the assignee are notified of every comment.
tasks.p4: Under the comments, the history shows who created, assigned, moved, re-prioritized or edited the task, and when.
tasks.p5: When a task turns into a bigger issue, turn it into a service-desk ticket with one click; the task is ticked off.
tasks.e1: The team lead adds "Verify documents of 12 new drivers", assigns it to Ravi, due Friday, priority Normal.
tasks.e2: Ravi sees it under Assigned to me and gets a notification.
tasks.e3: He comments "9 done, 3 are waiting for clearer photos", and the lead is notified.
tasks.e4: On Friday he marks it done. The history shows when it was assigned and when it was finished.

notes.summary: My notes is your private notebook for things to remember: contacts, steps, ideas. Only you can see them.
notes.p1: Write a title and the details, and add labels (for example bank, vendor) so you can find the note later.
notes.p2: Pin a note to keep it at the top of the list.
notes.p3: Search finds notes by their words.
notes.p4: When a note becomes work, turn it into a to-do or a service-desk ticket with one click.
notes.e1: You write "Bank escalation contacts" with the names and numbers, add the labels bank, escalation and pin it.
notes.e2: It stays at the top, so you find it in seconds during an incident.
notes.e3: A note "Refund rules unclear for cancelled trips" becomes a ticket for the Finance queue.

handover.summary: Handover notes pass the state of work from one shift to the next, so nothing is lost at shift change.
handover.p1: At the end of your shift, write what happened, what is still open and what the next shift must watch, and choose the shift it closes (morning, evening or night).
handover.p2: Tick the open tickets you are handing over, so the next shift can see them straight from the note.
handover.p3: The next shift clicks Mark as read. The note shows who has read it, so you know the handover landed.
handover.p4: Everyone on the team sees the handover notes, newest first.
handover.e1: At 22:00 Priya closes the evening shift: "2 payout failures still open, app sign-in slow since 20:30, watching it". She ticks OPS-57 and OPS-61.
handover.e2: Arjun starts the night shift, reads it and clicks Mark as read. Priya's note now shows "Read by Arjun".
handover.e3: Arjun picks up OPS-61 from the service desk and carries on.
